nodes.title: Formalizing inverse problems in the age of AI: possibilities, pitfalls, and an invitation
nodes.tldr: arXiv:2611.06962v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Proof assistants such as Lean check mathematical proofs down to the axioms, and AI agents have recently made writing such proofs che...
nodes.details: arXiv:2611.06962v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Proof assistants such as Lean check mathematical proofs down to the axioms, and AI agents have recently made writing such proofs cheap. We describe AutoIP, a Lean library in which classical linear regularization theory, together with the functional analysis it rests on, has been autoformalized by AI agents. A machine-checked proof certifies only the formal statement it proves, so the remaining human task is to confirm that each formal statement says what was intended. We organize the library around this task: a reviewer compares the formal statements with their natural-language counterparts and never needs to read a proof. Our experience is that the risks lie in the statements rather than in the proofs, and that simple automated tests on the statements can expose problems even in the established literature. We illustrate this with a textbook theorem whose hypothesis is more restrictive than asserted. We invite the inverse problems community to extend and build on the library.

nodes.title: KDASO: Knowledge-Data Dual-Driven Automated Skill Optimization for Liability Adjudication Tasks
nodes.tldr: arXiv:2611.06972v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Liability adjudication tasks (e.g., legal charge determination) require analyzing event descriptions against domain-specific skills ...
nodes.details: arXiv:2611.06972v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Liability adjudication tasks (e.g., legal charge determination) require analyzing event descriptions against domain-specific skills to determine whether a party should bear liability. While Large Language Models (LLMs) have shown promise in this area by leveraging executable skills for interpretable reasoning, existing approaches face three critical limitations: skill libraries become stale as real-world scenarios dynamically evolve, skill descriptions often suffer from a semantic execution gap where LLMs deviate from intended expert logic, and growing skill collections exceed context budgets causing critical skill omission. To address these challenges, we propose Knowledge-Data Dual-Driven Automated Skill Optimization (KDASO), which continuously evolves a skill library through neighborhood-conditioned induction from recent adjudication data, execution-aligned refinement based on LLM trajectory analysis, and context-budgeted routing for scalable skill selection. Experiments across ride-hailing adjudication, legal liability determination, and logical reasoning judgment demonstrate that KDASO significantly outperforms current general-purpose and domain-specific baselines. KDASO further achieves 8.96% improvement when transferring skills to concept-similar scenarios and maintains consistent performance gains through continuous optimization, underscoring the high transferability and stability of generated skills.

nodes.title: BlockLock: Reproducible LLM Inference with Fixed Batch Geometry
nodes.tldr: arXiv:2611.06977v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Reproducible LLM inference requires that a request produces the same output regardless of the other requests in the batch. Existing ...
nodes.details: arXiv:2611.06977v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Reproducible LLM inference requires that a request produces the same output regardless of the other requests in the batch. Existing solutions pay for this in different ways: batch-invariant kernels constrain every operator, and isolating prefill with fixed-shape decode ({our CoRun-style baseline}) gives up shared prefill compute and pads decode. We present BlockLock, which keeps shared batched prefill and pins only the numerical path of the protected request: it fixes the geometry that the request sees, with {two modes: BlockLock-Rows uses fixed-width rows and retains batched decode of all requests; BlockLock-Pack uses terminal-anchored packing with an isolated dummy segment, then extracts the protected request's KV state for target-only decode. Under a stated per-deployment contract, both modes preserve the target's output bitwise when its companions change.} Across five {dense} models (Qwen3-8B/14B, Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct, and Gemma-3-4B/12B-IT) and three single-GPU deployments (NVIDIA A6000, A100, and H100), we evaluate our approach on both tinyBenchmarks and BFCL{; we also include initial tensor-parallel experiments on two NVIDIA A6000 GPUs. Both modes preserve target sequences and Top20-logit bits in the reported tests.} At equal delivered work, {BlockLock-Rows} reduces latency by 53.5--55.0\% and improves throughput by 115.2--122.2\% relative to vLLM Batch-Invariant; compared with batch-invariant kernels, it needs no custom kernel implementations and constrains only the protected requests.

nodes.title: Resource-Efficient Reinforcement Learning Post-Training through Elastic Expert Parallelism
nodes.tldr: arXiv:2611.06984v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Reinforcement learning post-training improves the capabilities of large language models, but generating training responses is a majo...
nodes.details: arXiv:2611.06984v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Reinforcement learning post-training improves the capabilities of large language models, but generating training responses is a major computational bottleneck. In mixture-of-experts models, workers that finish their assigned responses may remain occupied because their experts are still needed by workers processing longer responses. Consequently, approximately one-third of occupied worker time in the baseline occurs after local response generation finishes. Here we present FlexFloor, a system that enables earlier resource release during synchronous response generation while preserving the expert computation required by ongoing responses. FlexFloor jointly adapts response scheduling and the active group of workers. It uses historical response lengths and memory constraints to guide batching and prompt placement, then progressively releases workers while maintaining expert availability and correct communication. Compared with the verl baseline, FlexFloor generates approximately 65.40% more response tokens per unit of occupied computing time and increases response generation throughput by 52.74%, with little observed variation in rollout reward. By making reinforcement learning post-training more efficient, FlexFloor supports faster development and iterative improvement of large language models and AI agents.

nodes.title: The Two-Ledger Model: Transaction-Grain Cost Accounting for Multi-Agent AI Systems Across Clouds, Mo
nodes.tldr: arXiv:2611.06989v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Enterprises run business transactions through multi-agent AI systems spanning clouds, large language models (LLMs), orchestration ha...
nodes.details: arXiv:2611.06989v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Enterprises run business transactions through multi-agent AI systems spanning clouds, large language models (LLMs), orchestration harnesses, and systems of record. Finance receives AI cost only at settlement grain, aggregated by SKU and charge period. The business question (what did this order, claim, or case cost in AI?) cannot be answered from billing data, because providers never see enterprise transaction boundaries. The FinOps Open Cost and Usage Specification (FOCUS) gives billing data one schema across providers but remains settlement-grain even as it adds AI token and requester attribution. We formalize this grain mismatch, derive seven requirements, and propose the Two-Ledger Model: a settlement ledger of FOCUS-conformant billing data joined to an attribution ledger of invocation-grain usage records built on OpenTelemetry GenAI telemetry. A layered correlation spine (trace context, A2A/MCP metadata, business-key correlation, probabilistic matching) assigns each record to its business transaction with recorded method and confidence; a versioned rate card prices usage in near real time; period reconciliation ties both ledgers to the invoice, and the unexplained residual identifies shadow AI. Costs are reported per order, claim, or outcome with agentic cost metrics. A simulation with known ground truth shows the spine sustaining cost coverage above 99% as trace propagation falls to zero, the reconciliation residual recovering planted unmetered spend within 0.24 percentage points while flagging provider billing errors, and mid-flight gating cutting p99 transaction cost by up to 61% at a 2-4% false-pause rate. We propose the attribution ledger as an invocation-grain FOCUS profile for standardization.

nodes.tldr: What about mob/ensemble programming? I work on a team that used to use mob programming heavily. There would be a driver and a navigator, and then someone taking notes. Other people...
nodes.details: What about mob/ensemble programming? I work on a team that used to use mob programming heavily. There would be a driver and a navigator, and then someone taking notes. Other people would be "muses" or observers. Always occurring over Zoom. I always felt like this was a very draining way of programming. Pair programming felt a bit better. Of course, we still get together to discuss architecture or how we want to go about a certain set of work or if we're blocked, but with agents, it just doesn't make sense to get everybody in a call to watch someone else's agent work.So, in the age of agentic AI, how do these two concepts evolve (or disappear)? nodes.title: CISA Adds One Known Exploited Vulnerability to Catalog
nodes.tldr: CISA has added one new vulnerability to its Known Exploited Vulnerabilities (KEV) Catalog, based on evidence of active exploitation. CVE-2026-19868 SonicWall SonicOS SSLVPN Us...
nodes.details: CISA has added one new vulnerability to its Known Exploited Vulnerabilities (KEV) Catalog, based on evidence of active exploitation. CVE-2026-19868 SonicWall SonicOS SSLVPN Use of Single-factor Authentication Vulnerability This type of vulnerability is a frequent attack vector for malicious cyber actors and poses significant risks to the federal enterprise. Binding Operational Directive (BOD) 26-04: Prioritizing Security Updates Based on Risk establishes vulnerability management requirements for Federal Civilian Executive Branch (FCEB) agencies. BOD 26-04 reinforces the importance of the KEV Catalog and requires federal agencies to prioritize rapid remediation of high-risk vulnerabilities, specifically those identified by Common Vulnerabilities and Exposures (CVEs) listed in CISA’s KEV Catalog on publicly exposed assets that grant total control of the asset post-exploitation, while deferring action for lower-risk vulnerabilities. BOD 26-04 further establishes basic expectations for when agencies must check whether threat actors compromised the system before the patch was applied. While BOD 26-04 applies only to FCEB agencies, CISA encourages all organizations to adopt risk-based vulnerability management and prioritize remediation of KEV Catalog vulnerabilities. CISA will continue to add vulnerabilities to the catalog that meet the specified criteria. Aware of an exploited vulnerability not currently listed in the KEV Catalog? Submit it for potential addition through CISA’s KEV Nomination Form. Potential KEV additions must have a CVE ID, evidence of exploitation, and clear mitigation guidance.

nodes.title: US Government Partners Urge Hardening Industrial Refrigeration and Cold Chain Monitoring Systems
nodes.tldr: Overview The Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security Agency (CISA), Federal Bureau of Investigation (FBI), Health and Human Services (HHS), U.S. Department of Agriculture (USDA),...
nodes.details: Overview The Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security Agency (CISA), Federal Bureau of Investigation (FBI), Health and Human Services (HHS), U.S. Department of Agriculture (USDA), and the Department of Transportation (DoT)—hereafter referred to as “the authoring organizations”—are aware of malicious cyber activity targeting industrial refrigeration and cold chain monitoring systems globally. Organizations in the Healthcare and Public Health, Chemical, Food and Agriculture, and Transportation Systems Sectors widely use these systems, including in refrigerated transport services, for automated and remote monitoring of temperatures, continuous temperature logging, defrost cycle management, and energy optimization. The authoring organizations urge owners and operators to defend against this activity by using strong authentication, keeping systems updated, identifying any systems that are accessible from the internet, removing unnecessary remote access, and securing any necessary remote access. Threat The authoring organizations are aware of malicious cyber actors targeting electronic temperature controllers and commercial refrigeration controllers in retail grocery and cold storage facilities. The actors may exploit vulnerabilities or weaknesses in unpatched or internet-accessible controllers to remotely alter settings and force units into continuous heating and defrost cycles, which can cause widespread inventory loss and equipment hazards. Specifically, the actors may exploit these flaws through multiple vectors: Authentication bypass; Arbitrary code injection; and Weak configurations. Upon successful exploitation of the flaws, the actors could achieve the following effects: Change of temperature, which could: Affect the service life of the system; Create a fire hazard; Cause loss of inventory; or Indirectly harm consumers if products are consumed after unsafe storage. Loss of visibility into current temperatures (a denial-of-view condition). Mitigations The authoring organizations urge owners and operators to immediately take the following actions. These mitigations align with the Cross-Sector Cybersecurity Performance Goals (CPGs), developed by CISA and the National Institute of Standards and Technology (NIST). The CPGs provide a minimum set of practices and protections that CISA and NIST recommend all organizations implement: Eliminate public internet exposure: Do not expose control system devices and/or systems, particularly controller panels, to the internet [CPG 3.S]. Should remote access be necessary, protect it by using a firewall or edge device and updating it to the latest version to reduce security vulnerabilities. See CISA’s Internet Exposure Reduction Guidance and Defend the Edge: The Critical Importance of Edge Device Security for additional guidance on securing edge devices. Isolate operational technology (OT) devices: Create a dedicated OT virtual local area network (VLAN) to separate OT devices from business networks [CPG 3.I]. Enforce credential security: Change default passwords [CPG 3.A], strengthen passwords, and implement strong password policies [CPG 3.B]. Further, implement phishing-resistant multifactor authentication wherever feasible [CPG 3.F]. Apply patches: Keep device firmware up to date and establish a structured lifecycle management process to identify, retire, and replace legacy devices that are at end of life (EOL) and no longer supported by the manufacturer [CPG 2.A, 2.B]. See CISA’s BOD 26-04: Implementation Guidance for Prioritizing Security Updates Based on Risk and BOD 26-02: Mitigating Risk From End-of-Support Edge Devices for additional guidance. Restrict access: Define and maintain device and IP address allowlisting, limiting access to only those devices and IP addresses authorized to make changes [CPG 3.H]. Have reliable backups: Maintain current backups offsite and offline and test them [CPG 3.O]. Monitor and report: Enable logging [CPG 3.Q] and regularly review logs for unexpected activity. For OT assets where logs are non-standard or not available, collect network traffic and communications between the assets. Review setpoint ranges: Define and maintain reasonable setpoint limits for devices operating downstream of controllers to stay within safe ranges and establish alerting for deviations. Resources The authoring organizations strongly urge industrial refrigeration and cold chain monitoring system owners and operators to secure remote access to their OT systems. To strengthen system security, owners and operators should review the following resources and implement recommended mitigations: CISA: Primary Mitigations to Reduce Cyber Threats to Operational Technology CISA: Defend the Edge: The Critical Importance of Edge Device Security CISA: Internet Exposure Reduction Guidance United Kingdom’s National Cyber Security Centre and Partners: Secure Connectivity Principles for OT Contact Information The authoring organizations recommend U.S. organizations report suspicious or criminal activity related to information provided in this fact sheet: Contact CISA via CISA’s 24/7 Operations Center at contact@cisa.dhs.gov or 1-844-Say-CISA (1-844-729-2472). For more information on reporting a cyber incident, refer to CISA’s Voluntary Cyber Incident Reporting web page. File a claim with FBI’s Internet Crime Complaint Center (IC3) or contact your local FBI field office. When available, please include the following information regarding the incident: Date, time, and location of the incident; Type of activity; Number of people affected; Type of equipment used for the activity; and Name of the submitting company or organization, and a designated point of contact. Contact HHS via HHSCyber@hhs.gov or the HHS 24/7 Operations Center at 202-619-7800 for assistance mitigating potential disruptions to the delivery of healthcare resulting from health and medical supply chain impacts. nodes.title: Post-Quantum Questions to Ask Your Vendors
nodes.tldr: CISA, the Australian Signals Directorate’s Australian Cyber Security Centre (ASD’s ACSC) and the National Security Agency (NSA) released joint guidance and an accompanying quick-re...
nodes.details: CISA, the Australian Signals Directorate’s Australian Cyber Security Centre (ASD’s ACSC) and the National Security Agency (NSA) released joint guidance and an accompanying quick-reference list to help organizations assess vendor readiness for transitioning to post-quantum cryptography (PQC). As quantum computing advances, widely used public-key cryptography will become vulnerable to compromise from cryptographically relevant quantum computers (CRQCs). To protect their systems and data, organizations must plan for and transition to PQC—which includes algorithms capable of withstanding both classical computing and quantum-enabled threats—before CRQCs become available.  Many organizations rely on third-party vendors for managed services, cloud capabilities, and other cryptography-dependent products and services. Cryptography is also embedded in systems and devices that are difficult to update, tied to long asset lifecycles, and require vendor support or replacement—such as industrial control systems and Internet of Things (IoT) devices. Reliance on vendors means that effective PQC transition depends on vendor readiness, and early, structured engagement with these vendors is critical to planning efforts.  Organizations can use the vendor-neutral questions outlined in this guidance to determine whether a vendor understands quantum-related risks, maintains transparency over its cryptographic implementations, and supports a secure, cost-effective and timely transition to PQC.  Visit CISA’s PQC Initiative page for additional resources.

nodes.title: Commission preliminarily finds TikTok’s ‘For You’ feed in breach of Digital Services Act for harmful
nodes.tldr: Commission preliminarily finds TikTok’s ‘For You’ feed in breach of Digital Services Act for harmful ‘rabbit holes’ effect Anonymous (not verified) Fri, 11/06/2026 - 12:09 The Euro...
nodes.details: Commission preliminarily finds TikTok’s ‘For You’ feed in breach of Digital Services Act for harmful ‘rabbit holes’ effect Anonymous (not verified) Fri, 11/06/2026 - 12:09 The European Commission has preliminarily found TikTok in breach of the Digital Services Act (DSA) for the so-called ‘rabbit hole effect’ of its recommender system. TikTok's ‘For You' feed shows users a continuous stream of personalised videos, even when those are related to mental health struggles and body image. The more a user interacts with a certain type of content, the more TikTok's ‘For You' feed algorithm recommends similar content. This design can be harmful when such endless and repeated exposure involves, for example, content about sadness, isolation or body image. These ‘rabbit holes' can have a detrimental impact on users' mental health, especially that of vulnerable adults and minors. These preliminary findings focus on both risk assessment and mitigation measures. nodes.title: Independent study on the impact of age assurance on fundamental rights and costs for businesses
nodes.tldr: Independent study on the impact of age assurance on fundamental rights and costs for businesses Anonymous (not verified) Wed, 11/04/2026 - 15:04 An independent study analyses the i...
nodes.details: Independent study on the impact of age assurance on fundamental rights and costs for businesses Anonymous (not verified) Wed, 11/04/2026 - 15:04 An independent study analyses the impacts of age assurance on fundamental rights and the costs for businesses concerned. Age assurance is key for a safer online environment as it ensures that children only access online services and features that are safe and age appropriate for them. Nowadays, 1 in 3 children, aged 9 to 11 across 6 European countries, reports having a social media profile. Very few services are implementing age assurance in a systematic way. To further strengthen the preparation of the proposed EU KIDS Act and the accompanying Staff Working Document, the European Commission procured a study to: Analyse the impact of age assurance on key fundamental rights, including data protection and privacy, non-discrimination, freedom of expression and access to information; Assess the potential financial impacts of age assurance on businesses, including micro and small enterprises. The study was carried out by an external contractor. It does not assess the proposed EU KIDS Act and the compliance by any specific service provider. The study's key insights are: Fundamental rights – an age assurance framework can be both proportionate and respectful of fundamental rights. Interferences with those rights can be mitigated through appropriate safeguards. In particular, the framework should ensure: Data protection and privacy – legislative coherence with the GDPR, high standards of privacy and security, and the development of technical standards; Non-discrimination, freedom of expression and access to information – minimising friction for users, ensuring transparency, promoting user empowerment where appropriate through greater choice, and ensuring inclusivity and accessibility. EU approach to age verification – the EU age verification blueprint can make an important contribution to the development of a coherent EU-level approach to age assurance. Specifically, the findings suggest that: the blueprint has the potential to become one of the most affordable ways for service providers of all sizes to comply with age assurance requirements because it is privacy-preserving and open by design and its development costs have been publicly subsidised; the roll-out of the blueprint across all Member States should be accelerated; the provision and resourcing of effective fallback enrollment routes – including manual enrolment options at national and local level – should be ensured. Costs for businesses – online services would inevitably face new costs. However, these costs are likely to remain modest for most services and to decrease over time, due to: competition in the third-party vendor market, the emergence of technical standards, improvements in interoperability, the availability of the EU age verification blueprint. For small and medium-sized enterprises (SMEs), the study suggests that it's unlikely to face excessive costs, thanks to affordable, ready-to-use age verification solutions and competition between providers. They will also benefit from having a common set of EU rules, rather than having to comply with different national requirements. Read the study and its executive summary and the questions & answers on the proposed EU KIDS Act. Related topics Online platforms and e-commerce DSA - Digital Services Act

nodes.title: Call for evidence on advertising repositories
nodes.tldr: Call for evidence on advertising repositories Anonymous (not verified) Wed, 11/04/2026 - 11:10   Opening: 04 November 2026   Closing: 02 December 2026 The Commission is s...
nodes.details: Call for evidence on advertising repositories Anonymous (not verified) Wed, 11/04/2026 - 11:10   Opening: 04 November 2026   Closing: 02 December 2026 The Commission is seeking feedback on upcoming technical guidelines concerning advertising repositories under the Digital Services Act (DSA). The feedback is being gathered through a call for evidence. The responses collected through the call for evidence will help shape guidelines aimed at ensuring that advertising repositories meet the needs of their users. Amongst other things, the guidelines will advise on: how to make advertising repositories easily searchable how to provide insights on how users are targeted and reached how to make the content of advertisements accessible Once adopted, these guidelines will aim to ensure that the advertising repositories provided by very large online platforms (VLOPs) and very large online search engines (VLOSEs) are effective and fit for purpose. Effective advertising repositories are essential tools for enabling greater public scrutiny of online advertising. Transparency in advertising – revealing who pays and how citizens are targeted – helps to protect public health, ensure a high level of consumer protection and safeguard the integrity of elections. Advertising repositories also support effective supervision and enforcement of the DSA. Next steps The call for evidence will be followed by a targeted public consultation in 2027. Researchers, civil society, providers of VLOPs and VLOSEs and representatives from the advertising industry will be invited to share feedback on a draft version of the guidelines. The publication of the guidelines is planned for the second quarter of 2028. Background Under Article 39 of the DSA, providers of VLOPs and VLOSEs are required to maintain publicly accessible repositories of advertisements displayed on their services. These repositories (commonly known as ‘ad libraries’) provide information on the content of advertisements, who paid for them, the period during which they were displayed, how many users the advertisements reached, and the main criteria used to decide who saw the advertisements. Article 39(3) of the DSA provides the possibility for the Commission to issue guidelines on the design of advertising repositories, following consultation with the European Board for Digital Services, researchers and the public. The guidelines will support the Commission’s supervision and enforcement of VLOPs and VLOSEs’ compliance with Article 39 of the DSA.
